classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied factorisation and gradient to combine parameter conditions for real intercepts and opposite-side turning points, including exceptional repeated-root cases; the hint supplies the main analytical representations.

content.prompt:
For what values of $a$ does the graph of $y=x^3+ax^2+ax+1$ look like the following?

Use the stated conditions as well as the unscaled sketches.

Hint: The gradient at $x$ is $G(x)=3x^2+2ax+a$. A turning point occurs where $G(x)=0$ and the gradient changes sign. If $G(x)>0$ for every real $x$, the graph has positive gradient everywhere. You may use $P(x)=(x+1)(x^2+(a-1)x+1)$ and complete the square in $G(x)$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The gradient is positive everywhere, and the gradient at the $y$-intercept is less than $1$.

spec.description: Increasing cubic, negative x-intercept, positive y-intercept and shallow region above the x-axis just left of the y-axis. No numerical ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: Equation-driven qualitative representative of the supplied family with internal reconstruction parameter a=1/2. This parameter is not a student-visible given and does not establish the requested interval.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied qualitative graph only; no parameter value or numerical coordinate labels.

answer.short:
$0<a<1$.

Use the supplied gradient and its value at $x=0$.
answer.worked:
Using the supplied gradient,
$$G(x)=3\left(x+\frac a3\right)^2+\frac{a(3-a)}3.$$
Positive gradient everywhere requires $a(3-a)>0$, so $0<a<3$. At the $y$-intercept, $G(0)=a<1$. Together these give $0<a<1$. For this interval, the quadratic factor of $P(x)$ has discriminant $(a-3)(a+1)<0$, so the only real zero is $-1$, as in the sketch.

children.label: b
children.prompt: There is exactly one $x$-intercept and two turning points, one on each side of the $y$-axis.

spec.description: Positive-leading cubic with one negative x-intercept, a maximum left of the y-axis and a minimum right of it, both above the x-axis. No numerical ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: Equation-driven qualitative representative of the supplied family with internal reconstruction parameter a=-1/2; that parameter is not printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied graph only; parameter answer hidden.

answer.short:
$-1<a<0$.

Combine the one-intercept condition with opposite-sign turning-point coordinates.
answer.worked:
$$P(x)=(x+1)\bigl(x^2+(a-1)x+1\bigr).$$
The quadratic factor has discriminant $(a-3)(a+1)$. Apart from the exceptional triple-root case $a=3$, exactly one $x$-intercept requires $-1<a<3$.
The turning-point coordinates are roots of the supplied equation $G(x)=3x^2+2ax+a=0$. Their product is $\frac{a}{3}$. Opposite signs require $a<0$, which also gives two distinct gradient zeros and sign changes. Hence $-1<a<0$. The case $a=3$ has no two turning points and is excluded.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The gradient is positive everywhere, and the gradient at the $y$-intercept is greater than $1$.

spec.description: Increasing cubic with negative x-intercept and positive y-intercept. Its shallow region lies near the negative x-intercept, lower and farther left than in graph (a). No numerical ticks or grid.

answer.short:
$1<a<3$.

Use the supplied gradient and its value at $x=0$.
answer.worked:
$$G(x)=3\left(x+\frac a3\right)^2+\frac{a(3-a)}3.$$
Positive gradient everywhere requires $0<a<3$. At the $y$-intercept, $G(0)=a>1$. Together these give $1<a<3$. The quadratic factor of $P(x)$ has discriminant $(a-3)(a+1)<0$, so the only real zero is $-1$, consistent with the sketch.

spec.description: Positive-leading cubic crosses at a negative x-value, has a maximum left of the y-axis, touches the x-axis at a positive minimum and rises. No numerical ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: The supplied family at a=-1 is (x+1)(x-1)^2, with a simple negative zero and a double positive zero.
spec.answerVisibility: No numerical roots or parameter answer printed.

answer.short:
$a=-1$.

The positive $x$-intercept is a double root.
answer.worked:
$$P(x)=(x+1)\bigl(x^2+(a-1)x+1\bigr).$$
The graph touches the $x$-axis at a positive zero. The quadratic factor must have a repeated positive root.
$$\begin{align*}(a-1)^2-4&=0\\a-1&=\pm2\\a&=-1\text{ or }3.\end{align*}$$
For $a=3$, $P(x)=(x+1)^3$, which has a triple negative zero and does not match the sketch.
For $a=-1$, $P(x)=(x+1)(x-1)^2$, which crosses at $x=-1$ and touches at $x=1$.
Hence $a=-1$.
